where: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Pedestrian signals help pedestrians cross at intersections with traffic lights.
The signal for pedestrians to walk is a white walking symbol.
A flashing or steady orange hand symbol means pedestrians must not begin to cross.

where: Pedestrian signals › Intro · image
Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶2

sentences.text: A pedestrian facing a walk signal may cross the road in the direction of the signal.
While crossing, pedestrians have the right-of-way over all vehicles.

where: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶3

sentences.text: A pedestrian facing a flashing or steady hand symbol should not begin to cross the road.
Pedestrians who have already begun to cross when the hand signal appears, should go as quickly as possible to a safe area.
While they are crossing, pedestrians still have the right-of-way over vehicles.

where: Pedestrian signals › Intro · image
figure: a pedestrian do not walk signal

where: Pedestrian signals › Intro · ¶4

sentences.text: At intersections with traffic lights where there are no pedestrian signals, pedestrians facing a green light may cross.
Pedestrians may not cross on a flashing green light or a left-turn green arrow.

where: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶1

sentences.text: Where there are pedestrian push-buttons, a pedestrian must use the button to bring on the walk signal.
Pedestrian signals give people more time to cross than regular traffic lights.
On a busy main road, an intersection pedestrian signal helps people to cross the road safely by signalling traffic to stop.
The intersection pedestrian signal has one or more crosswalks; pedestrian walk and don't walk signals; push buttons for pedestrians; and, traffic signal lights on the main road only.
Stop signs control traffic on the smaller, less busy crossroad.

where: Pedestrian signals › Intersection pedestrian signals · ¶2

sentences.text: You must observe, obey the traffic rules and use safe driving skills to drive through these intersections.
See also the section on driving through intersections .

where: Pedestrian signals › Summary · item 1

sentences.text: What the symbols on pedestrian signals indicate

where: Pedestrian signals › Summary · item 2

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Pavement markings combine with road signs and traffic lights to give you important information about the direction of traffic and where you may and may not travel.
Pavement markings divide traffic lanes, show turning lanes, mark pedestrian crossings, indicate obstacles and tell you when it is not safe to pass.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶2

sentences.text: Yellow lines separate traffic travelling in opposite directions.
White lines separate traffic travelling in the same direction.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: a four-lane highway with double solid yellow lines for opposing traffic and white broken lines for same-way traffic

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶3

sentences.text: A solid line at the left of your lane means it is unsafe to pass.
('A' should not pass.)

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: vehicles travelling beside a solid yellow line

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶4

sentences.text: A broken line at the left of your lane means you may pass if the way is clear.
('A' may pass if there are enough broken lines ahead to complete the pass safely.)

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: vehicles travelling beside broken yellow lines

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶5

sentences.text: Broken lines that are wider and closer together than regular broken lines are called continuity lines.
When you see continuity lines on your left side, it generally means the lane you are in is ending or exiting and that you must change lanes if you want to continue in your current direction.
Continuity lines on your right mean your lane will continue unaffected.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: three examples of continuity lines on on-ramps and off-ramps

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶6

sentences.text: A stop line is a single white line painted across the road at an intersection.
It shows where you must stop.
If there is no stop line marked on the road, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not.
If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.
If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: a stop line at an intersection

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶7

sentences.text: A crosswalk is marked by two parallel white lines painted across the road.
However, crosswalks at intersections are not always marked.
If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk.
If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.
If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
Pavement markings › Intro · ¶8

sentences.text: A white arrow painted on a lane means you may move only in the direction of the arrow.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: white directional arrows at an intersection

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶9

sentences.text: Pedestrian crossovers are identified by specific signs, overhead yellow lights, and pavement markings.
Pedestrian crossovers are marked by two white double parallel lines across the road with an X in each lane approaching it.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · ¶10

sentences.text: Drivers and cyclists must stop before the line and yield to pedestrians until pedestrians have completely crossed the road and cleared the roadway.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
Pavement markings › Intro · ¶11

sentences.text: Two solid lines painted on the pavement guide traffic away from fixed objects such as bridge piers or concrete islands.
Yellow and black markings are also painted on the objects themselves as warnings.

where: Pavement markings › Intro · image
figure: solid yellow lines around an object and yellow and black warning markings on objects

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Ontario has a one-piece driver’s licence.
The licence card has a photograph and signature of the driver.
All drivers in Ontario should have a one-piece licence card.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Intro · ¶2

sentences.text: You must carry your licence with you whenever you drive.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Renewing your licence · ¶1

sentences.text: You will get a renewal application form in the mail.
Take the form into any ServiceOntario Centre in the province.
They are all equipped to take photographs.
You will be asked to sign the form, show identification, pay a fee and have your photograph taken.
You will get a temporary licence on the spot if your application and documents are in order, and your permanent one will be mailed to you.
You must carry it with you whenever you drive and produce it when a police officer requests it.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Renewing your licence · ¶2

sentences.text: If you do not get a renewal application form in the mail when your licence is due for renewal, call the Ministry of Transportation.
You are responsible for making sure you have a valid driver’s licence.
You can renew an expired car or motorcycle driver’s licence within one year without taking any tests.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Renewing your licence · ¶3

sentences.text: If your licence has been suspended, cancelled or expired for more than three years, you will be required to re-apply for a licence in Ontario and meet all the requirements of graduated licensing, including passing all the required tests.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶1

sentences.text: If you are 80 years of age or older, you are required to renew your driver’s licence every two years.
This renewal process helps keep seniors mobile and independent longer, while helping to ensure that unsafe drivers are identified and appropriate actions are taken.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶2

sentences.text: Before your licence expires, you will receive a driver’s licence renewal application form and a letter in the mail explaining the steps you need to complete.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶3

sentences.text: First, you should:

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 1

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 2

sentences.text: review the rest the Official Ministry of Transportation Driver’s handbook

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 3

sentences.text: visit Ontario.ca/seniordriver for further details

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶4

sentences.text: Your next step is to book an appointment at a ServiceOntario centre, which you can do:

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 4

sentences.text: online: book a ServiceOntario appointment

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 5

sentences.text: by calling toll-free at 1-800-396-4233

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 6

sentences.text: by calling 416-235-3579 in the Greater Toronto area

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶5

sentences.text: At the appointment you will be required to complete a vision test and a five minute screening exercise.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶6

sentences.text: After the session, if you successfully complete all the requirements, you will be able to renew your licence.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶7

sentences.text: However, you may also need to pass a road test, follow up with your doctor and submit medical information or provide additional vision information from a doctor or optometrist before being able to renew your licence.
If additional medical information is required, you will be notified by mail.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶8

sentences.text: There is no charge for any of the licence-renewal requirements.
You only have to pay the licence-renewal fee.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · ¶9

sentences.text: More information relating to senior drivers can be found at Ontario.ca/seniordriver .
You can also:

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 7

sentences.text: call toll free at 1-800-396-4233

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › Licensing · item 8

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · ¶1

sentences.text: Your health is a key factor in your ability to drive.
To help you handle the demands of safe driving:

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 1

sentences.text: Check with your doctor or pharmacist to make sure current and new medications will not negatively affect your ability to drive.
Over-the-counter drugs and combinations of drugs can also impair your driving.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 2

sentences.text: Report to your doctor:

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 3

sentences.text: vision changes, unexplained dizziness or fainting spells;

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 4

sentences.text: frequent, chronic or severe pain.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 5

sentences.text: Avoid driving if you're exper­iencing pain.
It can decrease your ability to concentrate and limit your movement behind the wheel.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 6

sentences.text: Have your hearing and eyes checked regularly.
Peripheral vision and depth perception tend to decline over the years.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 7

sentences.text: Your doctor can recommend an exercise program to improve flexibility and maintain strength, which can help your ability to drive safely.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Senior drivers age 80 or older › What you can do to make your driving safer · item 8

sentences.text: Consider taking a driver’s course to refresh your knowledge of the rules of the road and safe driving practices.

sentences.text: Your answers to these questions can help you decide whether to continue to drive, cut back to certain times such as daylight hours or stop driving altogether.
If you have checked one or more of the warning signs and are concerned about your driving ability, talk to your doctor or family and get their opinions.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Graduated licensing requalification · ¶1

sentences.text: Under graduated licensing, novice drivers (Class G1, G2, M1 and M2) progress through a two-step licensing process by completing the mandatory time periods for each level and passing the required road tests.
Except for Class M1, novice drivers have five years to complete the graduated-licensing process.

However, if your Class G1, G2 or M2 licence is about to expire and you have not completed the process, you can regain or retain the same class of licence by passing a test and paying the five-year licensing fee.
This is called “requalification.”
A notice is sent to Class G1, G2 and M2 drivers before their licence expiry date to inform them of their options.
If you do not complete the graduated-licensing process or requalify before your G1, G2 or M2 licence expires, you will not have a licence to drive, and you must reapply for a Level One licence.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Changing your name or address · ¶1

sentences.text: You must tell the Ministry of Transportation within six days of changing your name or address.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Changing your name or address · ¶2

sentences.text: You will need a new licence when you change your address.
You can change your address on the ServiceOntario website or you can take the change of information to a Driver and Vehicle Licence Issuing Office, or mail it to the Ministry of Transportation, P.O.
Box 9200, Kingston, ON , K7L 5K4.
The ministry will send you a new licence.
When you get it, destroy your old licence and carry the new one with you whenever you drive.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Changing your name or address · ¶3

sentences.text: When your name changes, you need a new licence.
Take the documents you must show (see the chart on this page) and your current licence to a Driver and Vehicle Licence Issuing Office.
A new photograph will be taken.
You will get a temporary licence to use until your permanent licence is mailed to you.
Carry it with you whenever you drive.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › Changing your name or address · ¶4

sentences.text: There is no charge for getting a new licence because you change your name or address.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system · ¶1

sentences.text: The demerit-point system encourages drivers to improve their behaviour and protects people from drivers who abuse the privilege of driving.
Drivers convict­ed of driving-related offences have demerit points recorded on their records.
Demerit points stay on your record for two years from the date of the offence.
If you accumulate too many demerit points, your driver’s licence can be suspended.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › New drivers - demerit-point system for Level One and Level Two drivers › Two or more points · ¶1

sentences.text: You will receive a warning letter.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › New drivers - demerit-point system for Level One and Level Two drivers › Six points · ¶1

sentences.text: You will receive a second warning letter encouraging you to improve your driving behaviour.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › New drivers - demerit-point system for Level One and Level Two drivers › Nine or more points · ¶1

sentences.text: Your licence will be suspended for 60 days from the date you surrender it to the Ministry of Transportation.
You can lose your licence for up to two years if you fail to surrender your licence.
After the suspension, the number of points on your record will be reduced to four.
Any extra points could again bring you to the interview level.
If you reach nine points again, your licence may be suspended for six months.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › New drivers - demerit-point system for Level One and Level Two drivers › Nine or more points · ¶2

sentences.text: As a Level One or Level Two driver, you will have your licence suspended if you accumulate nine or more demerit points during a two-year period.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › New drivers - demerit-point system for Level One and Level Two drivers › Nine or more points · ¶3

sentences.text: Note: If you are a novice driver and are convicted of violating any novice condition, an offence that is associated with four or more demerit points or receive a court-ordered suspension for an offence that would have resulted in four or more demerit points, you will receive the appropriate penalty and Novice Driver Escalating Sanction licence suspension.
However, the demerit points will be recorded as zero on your record, and will not be counted towards the accumulated demerit point system.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › Fully licensed drivers - demerit-point system for fully licensed drivers › Six points · ¶1

sentences.text: You will receive a warning letter recommending that you improve your driving skills.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › Fully licensed drivers - demerit-point system for fully licensed drivers › Nine points · ¶1

sentences.text: You will receive a second warning letter encouraging you to improve your driving behaviour.

where: Keeping Your Driver’s Licence › The demerit point system › Fully licensed drivers - demerit-point system for fully licensed drivers › 15 points · ¶1

sentences.text: Your licence will be suspended for 30 days from the date you hand over your licence to the Ministry of Transportation.
You can lose your licence for up to two years if you fail to surrender it.
After the suspension, the number of points on your driver’s record will be reduced to seven.
Any extra points could again bring you to the interview level.
If you reach 15 points again, your licence will be suspended for six months.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: To promote safe driving for Ontarians, the province has some of the strictest driving laws regarding driving while impaired by alcohol or drugs, careless driving, “stunt” driving, fleeing police or a collision scene, and so on.

In addition to lengthy suspensions for driving offences, court sanctions can quickly escalate and include fines in the tens of thousands of dollars, reinstatement fees, licence restrictions, lifetime bans and even jail time.

sentences.text: Your licence may also be suspended for the following reasons:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 1

sentences.text: Escalating sanctions

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 2

sentences.text: Zero Blood-Alcohol Concentration ( BAC ) for novice and young drivers

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 3

sentences.text: Medical suspension

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 4

sentences.text: Discretionary HTA suspensions

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 5

sentences.text: Mandatory HTA suspensions

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 6

sentences.text: Administrative driver’s licence suspension ( ADLS )

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 7

sentences.text: "Warn-range" suspension

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Suspensions · item 8

sentences.text: Novice-driver violations

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · ¶1

sentences.text: Escalating sanctions for novice drivers would apply if any of the following occurrences have taken place within a five-year period:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · item 1

sentences.text: Any repeat violations of novice restrictions

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · item 2

sentences.text: Any HTA convictions for four or more demerit points

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Escalating sanctions · item 3

sentences.text: Court-ordered licence suspensions.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶1

sentences.text: The risk of a fatality or serious injury is almost five times greater for vehicles crashing at 50 km/h or more above the posted highway limit.
The increase in risk is even greater on roads with lower posted limits.
For example, on roads with a posted limit of 60 km/h or less, the risk of a fatality or serious injury is almost eight times greater for vehicles colliding at 50 km/h or more above the posted limit.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶2

sentences.text: Other types of aggressive driving include:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 1

sentences.text: driving 40 km/h or more above the posted speed limit on roads with a speed limit less than 80km/h

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 2

sentences.text: driving 50 km/h or more above the posted speed limit

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 3

sentences.text: driving a motor vehicle to prevent another vehicle from passing

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 4

sentences.text: intentionally cutting off another vehicle

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 5

sentences.text: street racing

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · item 6

sentences.text: driving stunts

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶3

sentences.text: The use of a connected nitrous-oxide system while driving on a highway is prohibited.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – dangerous behaviours · ¶4

sentences.text: For information on the regulation, you can visit the ontario.ca/laws .

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Sanctions – careless driving · ¶1

sentences.text: Careless driving is defined as: driving without due care, attention or without reasonable consideration for other persons using the highway; and, anyone, who chooses to put themselves and other road users at risk by driving aggressively or carelessly.
If convicted of careless driving a driver can face tough sanctions.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Zero Blood-Alcohol Concentration (BAC) for novice and young drivers · ¶1

sentences.text: All drivers who are 21 and under, regardless of licence class, must have a BAC level of zero when operating a motor vehicle.
You will receive a 24-hour roadside driver-licence suspension.
If convicted, you could face a fine and at least a 30-day licence suspension.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Medical suspension · ¶1

sentences.text: All doctors must report the names and addresses of everyone 16 years or older who has a condition that may affect their ability to drive safely (for example, a stroke, heart condition or dizziness, among others).
Doctors report this information to the Ministry of Transportation, and it is not given to anyone else.
Your driver’s licence may be suspended until new medical evidence shows that the condition does not pose a safety risk.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Mandatory HTA suspensions · ¶1

sentences.text: Your licence will be suspended:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Mandatory HTA suspensions · item 1

sentences.text: If you fail to stop for a police officer (a minimum of five years)

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Mandatory HTA suspensions · item 2

sentences.text: If you don't pay a traffic fine when ordered by the court

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · ¶1

sentences.text: Your licence will be suspended immediately for 90 days:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · item 1

sentences.text: If your BAC is more than 80 milligrams in 100 millilitres of blood (.08)

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · item 2

sentences.text: If you fail or refuse to give a breath, blood, oral fluid or urine sample when asked by police

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · item 3

sentences.text: If you fail or refuse to perform physical co-ordination tests or submit to a drug evaluation when required by police

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Administrative driver’s licence suspension (ADLS) · ¶2

sentences.text: This suspension takes effect at the roadside or police station.
It is separate from any criminal charges or prosecution that may also take place.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · ¶1

sentences.text: Drivers who register a blood-alcohol concentration in the “warn range” of .05 to .08 pose an immediate danger to themselves and other road users.
If caught driving in the warn range, you will receive an immediate driver’s-licence suspension at the roadside:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · item 1

sentences.text: For three days for a first occurrence

where: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · item 2

sentences.text: For seven days for a second occurrence, and you must undergo a remedial alcohol-education program

where: Other ways to lose your licence › "Warn-range" suspension · item 3

sentences.text: Substantially increased penalties and sanctions for each subsequent occurrence

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Novice-driver violations · ¶1

sentences.text: Drivers holding novice licences must follow the specific rules for their class of licence.
If you violate any of the graduated-licensing conditions, your licence will be suspended for 30 days.
This suspension takes effect from the time you surrender your licence.
You can lose your licence for up to two years if you fail to hand it over.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 1

sentences.text: If you fail a driver’s re-examination

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 2

sentences.text: If you don't pay your reinstatement fee or administrative monetary penalty following a suspension

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 3

sentences.text: If your cheque for licence fees are not honoured by your bank

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Your licence will be cancelled: · item 4

sentences.text: If you voluntarily surrender your driver’s licence to the Ministry of Transportation, or it is surrendered or returned by another jurisdiction

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · ¶1

sentences.text: You will receive a one-year licence suspension the first time you are convicted of a Criminal Code offence.
Subsequent offences increase substantially to a lifetime ban from driving.
Convictions will remain on your driver’s record for a minimum of 10 years.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · ¶2

sentences.text: Your licence will be suspended if you are convicted of any of the following Criminal Code offences:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 1

sentences.text: Driving or having care and control of a vehicle, including boats, when your BAC is more than 80 milligrams per 100 millilitres of blood (.08)

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 2

sentences.text: Refusing to submit to a breath test for alcohol

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 3

sentences.text: Failing or refusing to provide a breath sample for roadside testing

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 4

sentences.text: Failing to remain at the scene of a collision

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 5

sentences.text: Dangerous driving

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 6

sentences.text: Causing death or bodily harm by criminal negligence

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Criminal Code suspensions · item 7

sentences.text: Failing to stop for police

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Remedial measures · ¶1

sentences.text: There are several types of remedial measures.
The mandatory Back on Track program is for all drivers convicted of impaired, driving-related Criminal Code offences.
Drivers with more than one “Warn Range” conviction will be required to take an alcohol-education and/or alcohol-treatment program.
If your driver’s licence has been suspended because of a Criminal Code conviction, your licence will remain suspended until you have completed the remedial requirements.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Driving under suspension · ¶1

sentences.text: You may not drive, under any circumstances, when your licence is suspended.
If you are convicted of driving while your licence is suspended for an HTA offence, you will face fines in the thousands of dollars.
The court may order you to spend up to six months in jail.
Six months will be added to your current suspension as well.
If you are found guilty of driving while your licence is suspended for a Criminal Code offence, you can face fines of tens of thousands of dollars and spend time in jail.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Driving while prohibited · ¶1

sentences.text: This is a prohibition order under the Criminal Code conviction.
When convicted of violation of the order, you will get a suspension of one year for a first offence or two years for a subsequent offence.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · ¶1

sentences.text: To counter the dangerous behaviours of impaired and suspended driving, Ontario law includes seven-day vehicle impoundments for:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · item 1

sentences.text: Drivers operating a vehicle while under a Highway Traffic Act licence suspension

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · item 2

sentences.text: Drivers caught without a required ignition interlock

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · item 3

sentences.text: All drivers caught with a BAC over .08, or who fail/refuse to comply with a demand made by a police officer under the Criminal Code of Canada

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · ¶2

sentences.text: If you are caught driving while your licence is suspended for a Criminal Code offence, the vehicle you are driving will be impounded for a minimum of 45 days.
These vehicle impoundments apply regardless of whether the vehicle is borrowed from a friend or family member, business, employer or is rented.
The owner of the vehicle must pay the towing and storage costs before the vehicle will be released.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Vehicle-Impoundment Program · ¶3

sentences.text: The Vehicle-Impoundment Program makes vehicle owners responsible for ensuring that anyone driving their vehicles is not suspended.
People loaning or renting their vehicles can verify that a driver’s licence is valid by phone or online.
You can also get a driver’s abstract at any Service Ontario centre.
There is a nominal fee for each licence checked.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶1

sentences.text: Driving when your ability is impaired by alcohol or a drug is a crime in Canada.
Your vehicle does not have to be moving; you can be charged if you are impaired behind the wheel, even if you have not started to drive.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶2

sentences.text: In circumstances involving possible impairment by a drug or a combination of alcohol and a drug, police can require a driver to:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 1

sentences.text: provide breath samples

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 2

sentences.text: perform standardized field sobriety tests

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 3

sentences.text: conduct a drug recognition evaluation

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · item 4

sentences.text: provide oral fluid, urine or blood samples for screening

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶3

sentences.text: If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶4

sentences.text: If you are 21 years of age and under, you must not drive if you have been drinking alcohol.
Your blood- alcohol level must be zero.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Impaired driving · ¶5

sentences.text: For more information on impaired driving measures in Ontario, please visit the Ministry of Transportation website at: www.mto.gov.on.ca/english/safety/impaired-driving.shtml

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Alcohol · ¶1

sentences.text: The police can stop any driver to determine if alcohol or drug testing is required.
They may also do roadside spot checks.
When stopped by the police, you may be told to blow into a machine that tests your breath for alcohol, a roadside screening device, or perform physical co-ordination tests.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Alcohol · ¶2

sentences.text: If you cannot give a breath sample or it is impractical to obtain a sample of breath, the police officer can require you to provide a blood sample instead.
The police may also require a driver to provide, blood, oral or urine samples.
If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · ¶1

sentences.text: Criminal Code and HTA sanctions apply to drivers impaired by alcohol or a drug.

In circumstances involving possible impairment by drugs or a combination of alcohol and a drug, police can require a driver to perform physical co-ordination tests and submit to a drug evaluation, and then require a driver to provide blood, oral fluid or urine samples.
If you fail or refuse to comply with any of these demands, you will be charged under the Criminal Code.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · ¶2

sentences.text: Some drugs that your doctor may prescribe for you and some over-the-counter drugs can also impair your driving.
Here are some points you should remember:

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 1

sentences.text: If you use prescription medicines or get allergy shots, ask your doctor about side effects such as dizziness, blurred vision, nausea or drowsiness that could affect your driving.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 2

sentences.text: Read the information on the package of any over-the-counter medicine, including cold, allergy, sedative or diet pills.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 3

sentences.text: Drugs and any amount of alcohol together can have dangerous effects, even several days after you have taken the drug.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Drugs · item 4

sentences.text: Do not take a chance; ask your doctor or pharmacist.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶1

sentences.text: Ontario leads the way in combating drinking and driving through some of the toughest laws and programs in North America, including licence suspensions, heavy fines, vehicle impoundment, mandatory alcohol-education and -treatment programs, and the ignition interlock program.
Depending on your number of prior convictions, you may be fined up to $50,000, serve time in jail or lose your licence permanently.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶2

sentences.text: For impaired driving that causes injury or death, the penalties are even more severe.
If you are convicted of impaired driving causing bodily harm, you may be sentenced to up to 14 years in prison.
Impaired driving causing death can carry a sentence of imprisonment for life.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶3

sentences.text: If you drink and drive and are involved in a collision, you may suffer serious injury or cause serious injury to someone else.
Your insurance company might not pay for your medical or rehabilitation costs, or for the damage to your or the other person’s vehicle.
Your insurance costs may rise significantly.
You may have to pay substantial legal costs as well.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Consider the consequences of impaired driving · ¶4

sentences.text: If you are required to drive on the job, a licence suspension could mean losing your employment.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Driver-improvement interview · ¶1

sentences.text: The other remedial-measures program is for drivers convicted of non-drinking-and-driving-related Criminal Code offences who have no previous alcohol-related convictions.
You must undergo a Ministry of Transportation driver-improvement interview.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Driver-improvement interview · ¶2

sentences.text: If you have not completed the driver-improvement interview by the time your Criminal Code suspension expires, your licence will be further suspended until you have completed the remedial requirements.

where: Other ways to lose your licence › Driver-improvement interview · ¶3

sentences.text: This program also applies to Ontario residents convicted of driving-related Criminal Code offences in any other province of Canada, or equivalent offences in the states of Michigan and New York, as well as to out-of-province drivers who are convicted in Ontario.

where: Your Vehicle › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: All motor vehicles on Ontario roads must be registered, insured and maintained to meet certain basic safety standards.
If you own a vehicle, you are responsible for making sure it meets the requirements.
People who buy and sell vehicles also have certain responsibilities.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: It is illegal to drive a vehicle in dangerous condition.
But maintaining your vehicle also makes sense from an economic point of view: it can mean better gas mileage and a better price when you sell it.
Maintaining your vehicle also helps to protect the environment.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Intro · ¶2

sentences.text: A police officer or Ministry of Transportation inspector can examine your vehicle, its equipment and any trailer attached to it, at any time.
If the vehicle is found to be unsafe, it may be taken off the road until the problem is fixed.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Intro · ¶3

sentences.text: The following driver habits and regular maintenance will help keep your vehicle fit and safe.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits · image
Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits · ¶1

sentences.text: Driver habits are the things that you can do whenever you drive a vehicle.
If you identify any concerns or deficiencies, further investigation or actions, including inspection and repair by a qualified mechanic, should be considered.
The vehicle’s owner manual often has detailed information on what to look for when inspecting your vehicle and how to address minor problems.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When approaching your vehicle look for signs of: · item 1

sentences.text: Fresh damage

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When approaching your vehicle look for signs of: · item 2

sentences.text: Fluid leaks underneath

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When approaching your vehicle look for signs of: · item 3

sentences.text: Under-inflated or flat tires

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When approaching your vehicle look for signs of: · item 4

sentences.text: Ajar doors, hood, trunk and fuel door/cap

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When approaching your vehicle look for signs of: · item 5

sentences.text: Unsecured loads

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When approaching your vehicle look for signs of: · item 6

sentences.text: Check for ice, snow, or dirt that may interfere with vehicle lighting, steering, driver visibility, or become a hazard to other motorists should it come free from your vehicle

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › From the driver’s seat and before driving, look for: · item 1

sentences.text: Unobstructed visibility around entire vehicle

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › From the driver’s seat and before driving, look for: · item 2

sentences.text: Burned-out or dim headlamps

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › From the driver’s seat and before driving, look for: · item 3

sentences.text: Illuminated dashboard warning lights during engine start, then going out

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › From the driver’s seat and before driving, look for: · item 4

sentences.text: Loose objects in the vehicle

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › While driving, be alert for: · item 1

sentences.text: Unusual engine or exhaust noises

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › While driving, be alert for: · item 2

sentences.text: Squeaking or grinding noises when applying the brakes

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › While driving, be alert for: · item 3

sentences.text: Dashboard warning lights coming on

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When planning an extended trip, perform more detailed checks, including: · item 1

sentences.text: Windshield wipers and washer-fluid level

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When planning an extended trip, perform more detailed checks, including: · item 2

sentences.text: Tire pressures, condition and wear

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When planning an extended trip, perform more detailed checks, including: · item 3

sentences.text: All lights work

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When planning an extended trip, perform more detailed checks, including: · item 4

sentences.text: Under the hood when the engine is cold; oil and coolant levels, obvious defects with belts, hoses, and possible leaks.
Using the vehicle owner’s manual for more information on what to look for

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Driver Habits › When planning an extended trip, perform more detailed checks, including: · item 5

sentences.text: Having your vehicle thoroughly inspected by a qualified mechanic

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Regular Maintenance · ¶1

sentences.text: In order to keep your vehicle running smoothly, vehicle manufacturers often establish a schedule for regular maintenance.
Scheduling of this work is normally based upon accumulated vehicle mileage or time intervals (whichever comes first).
Further details may be found in the vehicle’s owner’s manual.
Regular maintenance may include oil and filter change, other fluid checks and changes, air and fuel filter replacement, tire rotation and brake inspection.
Periodically, more intensive mechanical servicing such as engine adjustments and timing-belt replacement may be required.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · ¶1

sentences.text: A well-maintained vehicle will usually start in all weather conditions.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · ¶2

sentences.text: Carry emergency supplies.
These should include:

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · item 1

sentences.text: a shovel

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · item 2

sentences.text: booster cables

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · item 3

sentences.text: emergency flares or warning lights

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · item 4

sentences.text: a blanket

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · item 5

sentences.text: a chain for towing.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · ¶3

sentences.text: Always carry extra windshield washer fluid in the winter and refill the container when necessary.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Winter maintenance · ¶4

sentences.text: Faulty exhaust systems are especially dangerous in the winter when drivers are more likely to drive with windows and vents closed.
Have your exhaust checked if it sounds noisy or rattles.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · image
figure: a tire with bulges, cracks and worn spots

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · ¶1

sentences.text: The type of tires you have and the way they are made are critical for good traction, mileage and safety.
Keep these points in mind when you buy or replace tires, and check your vehicle owner’s manual or the tire manufacturer’s guide for recommendations.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · ¶2

sentences.text: Tires must meet standards described in the Canadian Motor Vehicle Safety Act .
Tires deteriorate with age, even when not in use.
Aged tires have reduced traction, are more prone to cracking and may fail unexpectedly while in use.
Tires should not be older than 10 years.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 1

sentences.text: Replace tires when the tread is less than 1.5 millimetres deep or when tread-wear indicators touch the road.
Vehicles that weigh more than 4,500 kilograms must replace their front tires when tread is less than three millimetres deep.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 2

sentences.text: Replace tires that have bumps, bulges, knots, exposed cords or tread and sidewall cuts deep enough to expose cords.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 3

sentences.text: Any tire on a vehicle must not be smaller than the vehicle manufacturer’s specified minimum size.
And it must not be so large that it touches the vehicle or affects its safe operation.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 4

sentences.text: You should use similar tires on all four wheels of your vehicle.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 5

sentences.text: To provide the best traction during the winter season, it is recommended that your vehicle be equipped with four winter or all-weather tires with the same tread pattern.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 6

sentences.text: If you live in northern Ontario, you can legally use studded tires on your vehicle.

where: Maintaining your vehicle › Tires · item 7

sentences.text: Scrap tires are a serious environmental concern.
Proper maintenance will extend the life of a tire and delay its disposal.
Some tips for longer wear: maintain the right air pressure; inspect tires for wear; rotate tires regularly and practice good driving habits.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Auto insurance – it’s the law! · ¶1

sentences.text: Ontario has compulsory automobile insurance.
This means every vehicle registered in the province must be insured.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Auto insurance – it’s the law! · ¶2

sentences.text: You must show proof that you have insurance coverage before you can register a vehicle or renew your registration.
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario ( FSRA ), regulates insurance in Ontario.
Visit FSRA 's website for more information on auto insurance.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶1

sentences.text: Vehicle registration includes licence plates and a vehicle permit.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶2

sentences.text: Licence plates in Ontario are based on a plate-to-owner system.
This means that vehicle licence plates move with the vehicle owner, not the vehicle.
When you sell or change vehicles, you must remove your plates.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶3

sentences.text: If you do not intend to use them on another vehicle, you may return your plates to a ServiceOntario centre.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Registration · ¶4

sentences.text: Learn more about buying, selling and registering a vehicle.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › New residents · ¶1

sentences.text: New Ontario residents have 30 days to register their vehicles.
To get a permit and Ontario licence plates, go to a ServiceOntario centre.
You must bring along:

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud · ¶1

sentences.text: By being vigilant, Ontario drivers can help put a stop to fraudsters who abuse the automobile insurance system.
Keep this in mind to protect yourself from auto insurance fraud.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › When Buying Auto Insurance: · item 1

sentences.text: Use a licensed insurance company, agent or broker.
The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario (FSRA), an agency of the Ministry of Finance, regulates insurance in Ontario.
Visit FSRA’s website, to check whether an insurance company or agent is licensed.
The Registered Insurance Brokers of Ontario (RIBO) is the self-regulatory body for insurance brokers in Ontario.
Visit RIBO’s website, to check whether an insurance broker is licensed.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 1

sentences.text: Collect as much information as possible.
Take photos of the collision scene.
Get the names, addresses, phone numbers, licence plate and driver’s licence numbers, and insurance information from all those involved in the collision, including passengers in the other vehicle(s).

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 2

sentences.text: Be suspicious of referrals.
Be wary if you are pressured or offered money by a tow truck operator to go to a particular body shop, lawyer, paralegal or health-care provider.
Contact your insurance company for information on towing and where to take your vehicle to be repaired.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 3

sentences.text: Refuse to sign blank forms in advance of receiving any services or health-care treatment related to your collision.

where: Vehicle insurance and registration › Protect yourself from auto insurance fraud › After an Auto Collision: · item 4

sentences.text: Demand detailed repair and medical bills for any goods and services related to your collision, and review them carefully.
